newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast's Amara Essy preaches U.N. reform.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast's Amara Essy preaches U.N. reform.

text.p: Ivorian Foreign Minister Amara Essy, one of four Africans bidding for the top job at the United Nations, said on Tuesday that the world body had to live within its means and its bureaucracy should be trimmed accordingly.

Essy, promoting himself as a reformist secretary-general, told reporters in Ivory Coast's commercial capital Abidjan, that he had already started efforts at reform when he was president of the U.N. general assembly in 1994 and 1995.
He said that if elected to succeed Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who has temporarily set aside his bid for a now traditional second term in the face of a U.S. veto, he would launch into "in-depth reform."
"The budget must be adapted to spending," Essy said, adding that he would cut the number of U.N. departments and find further cuts in staff numbers.

Essy, one of four candidates nominated by their respective governments on Friday, was Ivory Coast's permanent representative at the U.N. from 1981 to 1990. He presided over the general assembly's 49th annual session from September 1994 to September 1995.

The United States says Egypt's Boutros-Ghali has not done enough to reform the world body but that Africa should still have the right to the second five-year term. Ghana, Ivory Coast, Niger and Mauritania have formally nominated nationals as candidates for the post.
Essy said that when he was president of the general assembly a commission under his name had proposed reforms.

He acknowledged that Boutros-Ghali had cut staff numbers from 12,000 in 1994 to 8,500 in 1995 but added that further cuts were needed. "These are unpopular reforms and decisions, but they must be taken," he said.
He said certain institutions had outlived their usefulness, citing the U.N. Industrial Development Organisation UNIDO.
He added that it was "indispensable" that all member states pay their membership dues.

The Security Council was to conduct its first unofficial poll for the job later on Tuesday. Diplomats said there would be at least two rounds in what Council President Paolo Fulci of Italy termed an informal straw poll on the four names submitted.
To win, a candidate needs at least nine votes in the 15-seat council and no veto from any of its five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France.
Any candidate approved by the council must be endorsed by the 185-member General Assembly before December 31 when Boutros-Ghali's five-year term expires.
Essy said that the job required the twin qualities of manager and politician. "Political will and decisivenes are necessary," he added.

Asked about his qualities for the job, he cited his international experience, adding that he had been associated with the U.N. and its different organisations for about 20 years. "It's not unknown territory for me," he said.
